name: dopewars
desc: Free rewrite of a game originally based on "Drug Wars"
why: A 1984-descended terminal drug-dealing game, a rare old-school text game worth a browse even if the premise is dated.

brief.what_it_is: dopewars is a free Unix and Win32 rewrite of a game originally based on "Drug Wars" by John E. Dell. The player deals drugs on the streets of New York, aiming to build a large fortune and pay off a loan shark while avoiding the police. The homepage says it includes an "antique" mode that closely follows the original, plus multi-player games. The homepage describes the game and its features but does not say what input or output looks like in practice.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no separate rationale. It says the rewrite adds multi-player play and an antique mode that tracks the original Drug Wars, and that it aims to be highly configurable.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says that anything not changeable in the configuration files can be changed by editing the source, which is freely available under the GNU General Public License. It also mentions a Perl framework for writing AI clients, courtesy of Dave Madison, and a separate dopewars build with a behaviour-based AI. The homepage does not explain the client/server networking mechanism.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says dopewars runs on Unix systems (e.g. Linux, Solaris, Mac OS) and on Win32 (Windows 7 or later). The homepage has a Download page, but I could not reach it, so I have no installation steps, dependencies, or configuration first-run notes beyond the configuration files it mentions.
brief.standout: It is a free, open-source, multi-player take on a 1980s text-based drug-dealing game, and it keeps an antique mode that follows the original rules. The author also published an AI client framework in Perl and a version with a behaviour-based AI, so players can script bots against it.
brief.status: Maintained, per the homepage. It announces version 1.6.2, which adds Unicode support to the text-mode client and networking on Haiku. The page was last updated on Sat Dec 02 2023 (the year is taken from the page's timestamp). Its links point to a GitHub development repository and an open issue tracker. I could not confirm the latest commit date.
brief.caveats: The homepage advises that it is not recommended for children under 16 without parental supervision, and says the authors do not condone real-life drug dealing. The README I could reach is the homepage only. The GitHub repository URL I guessed returned 404, and a documentation URL I guessed also returned 404, so I have no command-line usage, options list, or build instructions. Windows support requires Windows 7 or later.
